# Overview
This demonstrates the full workflow provided by the package:

1. The Classic Budgeon Model: 

We replicate the methodology from Budgeon et al. (2017), which aggregates data from an entire cohort to build a single disease progression curve.

2. Advanced Model with Reliability Filtering: 

We showcase an enhanced workflow that first filters the cohort to include only "reliable accumulators." using annualized rate of change (ARC), then conduct time-to-positivity estimation following the classical model. 

To properly demonstrate both workflows, our `generate_synth_data()` function can produce data for each scenario.

```{r setup}
library(Budgeon)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
engine_to_use <- if (requireNamespace("cutpointr", quietly = TRUE)) "cutpointr" else "grid"
```

# Generate Synthetic Data
## Scenario 1: Data for the Classical Budgeon Model (exact replicate)

First, we generate data that mimics the simulation of Budgeon et al. (2017), where subjects have similar, low baseline biomarker levels (homogeneous baselines).
```{r}
df_classic <- generate_synth_data(n = 100, T = 50, l = 1, baseline_variability = "homogeneous")
#define parameters
id_name <- "ID"; time_name <- "Time"; value_name <- "Marker_level"
PET_pos_threshold <- 0.32   
degree <- 3
```
## Scenario 2: Data for the Complex Pipeline 
To demonstrate the complex pipeline with prior filtering, we need a dataset with varied (heterogeneous) baselines. This is the default and recommended setting.

```{r}
df_varied <- generate_synth_data(
  n = 100, T = 50, l = 1, 
  baseline_variability = "heterogeneous"
)
```

# The Classical Model (No Prioritize Filtering)
Here, we apply the standard pipeline to the `df_classic` dataset, using all subjects to construct the cohort curve, as described in the original paper.

```{r}
t2p_none <- get_Time_to_Positivity(
  df_classic, id_name, time_name, value_name, PET_pos_threshold,
  degree = degree, reliability_filter = "none"
)
head(t2p_none)
```

# Complex Pipeline with Prioritize Filtering
Now, we use the `df_varied` dataset to demonstrate the filtering workflow.

## Derived Filter (ARC -> value that max F1)
The pipeline automatically derives an optimal baseline biomarker cut-point to filter the cohort before building the model.
```{r}
t2p_derive <- get_Time_to_Positivity(
  df = df_varied,
  id_name, time_name, value_name, 
  PET_pos_threshold, 
  degree = degree,
  reliability_filter = "derived_value",
  engine = engine_to_use,
  seed = 321,
  verbose_filter = TRUE
)

# Show the results of the filtering
str(list(
  applied_mode    = t2p_derive$filter_info$applied_mode,
  value_threshold = t2p_derive$filter_info$thresholds$value_threshold,
  kept_ids        = t2p_derive$filter_info$n_kept,
  total_ids       = t2p_derive$filter_info$n_total
))

```

## User-defined Filter
Alternatively, a user can supply their own pre-defined threshold. This bypass the process of using ARC and F1 to calculate the biomarker threshold for reliable accumulation subject data. 
```{r}
user_defined <- 0.22 # Set by User

t2p_user <- get_Time_to_Positivity(
  df_varied, id_name, time_name, value_name, PET_pos_threshold,
  degree = degree,
  reliability_filter = "user_value",
  value_threshold = user_defined,
  verbose_filter = TRUE
)

list(
  user_defined = user_defined,
  kept_ids = t2p_user$filter_info$n_kept,
  total_ids = t2p_user$filter_info$n_total
)
```

# Visual checks
```{r}
make_four_panel <- function(df_long, title_prefix = "Cohort") {
  indiv <- get_individ_lm(df_long, value_name, time_name, id_name)
  indiv <- indiv[indiv$Slope >= 0, , drop = FALSE]
  eval  <- eval_lmm(df_long[df_long[[id_name]] %in% indiv[[id_name]], , drop = FALSE],
                    id_name = id_name, time_name = time_name, individual_coeffs = indiv)
  curve <- get_integration_estimates(eval, id_name = id_name, degree = degree)

  p1 <- ggplot(df_long, aes(x = .data[[time_name]], y = .data[[value_name]], group = .data[[id_name]])) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.8) + geom_line(alpha = 0.4) + theme_bw() +
    labs(x = "Time", y = "Marker Level", title = sprintf("%s: A. Longitudinal Data", title_prefix))

  p2 <- ggplot(eval, aes(x = eval_at_midpoint, y = Slope)) +
    geom_point() + theme_bw() + geom_smooth(method = "gam", se = FALSE, colour = "#782223") +
    labs(x = "Estimated Mean by Participant", y = "Estimated Slope", title = "B. Mixed-Effects Summary")

  p3 <- ggplot(curve, aes(x = mu_tau, y = tau)) +
    geom_point() + theme_bw() + geom_smooth(method = "gam", se = FALSE, colour = "#782223") +
    labs(x = "Marker Level", y = "Disease Progression Time", title = "C. Integrate reciprocal of B")

  p4 <- ggplot(curve, aes(x = tau, y = mu_tau)) +
    geom_point() + theme_bw() + geom_smooth(method = "gam", se = FALSE, colour = "#782223") +
    labs(x = "Disease Progression Time", y = "Marker Level", title = "D. Inversion of C")

  gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  invisible(curve)
}

# 1. Visualize the classic model on the full, unfiltered classic dataset
 make_four_panel(df_classic, "Classic Model (All IDs)")

# 2. Visualize the results of the derived filter on the varied-baseline dataset
make_four_panel(t2p_derive$filter_info$data, "Derived-Value Filtered")

```

# Cross-sectional Time to Positivity 

Once a cohort model is built, it can estimate the T2P for a new individual with a single measurement. It is important that the queried biomarker values fall within the range of the data used to build the model; the function will return`NA` for extrapolated values.

```{r}
mu_subject <-  c(0.40, 0.55, 0.60)    
mu_thresh  <- PET_pos_threshold

# We use the model built from the derived-filter cohort for this example.
t2a <- t2a_crosssectional(
  df = t2p_derive$filter_info$data, 
  id_name, time_name, value_name,
  mu_subject, mu_threshold = mu_thresh, degree = degree,
  reliability_filter = "none" # 'none' here because data is already filtered
)
data.frame(
  Subject_Value = mu_subject,
  Years_to_Positivity = t2a
)
```

# Conclusion

The `Budgeon` package provides a framework for modeling longitudinal biomarker data. This vignette has demonstrated how to:

1. Replicate the classic Budgeon et al. (2017) model using the entire cohort.

2. Apply an advanced reliability-accumulation filter using either a derived or user-defined threshold, which allows for more stable and reliable T2P calculation. 

3. Visualize the intermediate steps of the model for diagnostic checks.

4. Estimate time-to-positivity for new, cross-sectional subjects.
